Latent transition analysis with the latents R package

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/articles/lta.Rmd
lta.Rmd

Latent transition analysis (LTA) models change in latent states over repeated occasions (Collins & Lanza, 2010). At every occasion, each unit belongs to one of a small number of unobserved states, defined, as in latent class or profile analysis, by their distributions on the observed indicators. Change is the movement of units between these states from one occasion to the next. LTA estimates the states, how units are distributed over them at the start, and how likely each move is.

What latent transition analysis is

States are latent. The indicators measure the state of a unit at an occasion with error. Classifying each occasion separately, for instance with one latent profile analysis per occasion, and cross-tabulating the assignments treats every misclassification as a change of state and overstates instability. LTA estimates the states and the transitions in one model, so the transition probabilities are corrected for classification error under the model’s assumptions (Collins & Lanza, 2010).

The model has three parts. With SjtS_{jt} the state of unit jj at occasion tt and YjtY_{jt} its indicators,

  • the measurement model P(Yjt∣Sjt=k)P(Y_{jt} \mid S_{jt} = k) defines each state: means and variances for continuous indicators, response probabilities for categorical ones;
  • the initial probabilities δk=P(Sj1=k)\delta_k = P(S_{j1} = k) give the distribution of the states at the first occasion;
  • the transition probabilities τkl=P(Sjt=l∣Sj,t−1=k)\tau_{kl} = P(S_{jt} = l \mid S_{j,t-1} = k) give the probability of moving from state kk to state ll; each row of the transition matrix sums to one, the diagonal holds the probabilities of staying, and the off-diagonal cells the direction of change.

Default assumptions make the transitions interpretable. The measurement model is the same at every occasion (measurement invariance), so a state means the same thing throughout and a transition is a change of state rather than a change of the states’ definitions. The next state depends only on the current one (the first-order Markov property), and the transition probabilities are the same at every move (homogeneity). Each of these can be relaxed, as the last section shows.

LTA is a hidden Markov model. The states form a Markov chain that is not observed directly; only the indicators are. In the terminology of hidden Markov models (Rabiner, 1989), the measurement model gives the emission distributions. lta() estimates the model by maximum likelihood with the EM algorithm, computing the posterior probabilities of the states with the forward-backward recursions.

Group classes add heterogeneity in change. A single transition matrix assumes that all units change in the same way. With latent group classes, each class has its own initial and transition probabilities over the same states, a mixed Markov model (van de Pol & Langeheine, 1990). The classes are types of dynamics: for example, units that leave an unfavourable state quickly and units that remain in it. The mover-stayer model (Goodman, 1961) is the special case with one class of units that never change state.

The output describes change: the prevalence of each state over time, the stability of each state (the diagonal of the transition matrix), the most likely moves out of each state, the differences in dynamics between group classes and, with covariates, the predictors of the initial state and of each transition.

Data

course_engagement is simulated and has one row per course enrolment: 1,422 enrolments from 106 students. The simulation is calibrated to the engagement data of students followed through a full study programme (Saqr & López-Pernas, 2021; Saqr et al., 2023): its scales, spread, correlations and the persistence of engagement across courses follow those data, while no value of the source is retained. lta() needs three kinds of variables.

  • Group: student identifies whose occasions belong together.
  • Occasion order: sequence is the position of each course in the student’s history. Students can have different numbers of occasions (10 to 15 here).
  • Indicators: five activity measures (browse, lectures, forum_read, forum_post, attendance), each standardized within course, so 0 is the course average.

The data were generated from two engagement profiles and two kinds of students, committed and wavering, whose stationary probabilities of an engaged enrolment are about 0.8 and 0.25; engagement changes along each student’s sequence (?course_engagement). attendance is generated from the four click measures, so the indicators are correlated within profiles.

library(latents)
vars <- c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance")

Numbers of profiles and group classes

enumerate_classes() with time compares transition models. Because attendance depends on the other indicators, the candidates estimate full within-profile covariances (covariance_model = "full"); with a diagonal structure, an additional profile absorbs that dependence (see the multilevel latent profile analysis vignette).

grid <- enumerate_classes(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
                          time = "sequence", covariance_model = "full",
                          n_profiles = 2:3, n_group_classes = 1:3,
                          n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
#> 3 of 6 candidates reached their best log likelihood from one start only (profiles3_groups1, profiles3_groups2, profiles3_groups3); refit those you consider with more starts.
grid
#> Transition-model enumeration: 6 candidates (LTA)
#>          candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model log_likelihood n_parameters   bic   aic entropy
#>  profiles2_groups1          2               1  <NA>          -8206           43 16613 16499  0.9434
#>  profiles3_groups1          3               1  <NA>          -8172           68 16662 16481  0.9462
#>  profiles2_groups2          2               2  <NA>          -8188           47 16596 16471  0.9427
#>  profiles3_groups2          3               2  <NA>          -8159           77 16677 16472  0.8487
#>  profiles2_groups3          2               3  <NA>          -8187           51 16612 16476  0.9429
#>  profiles3_groups3          3               3  <NA>          -8151           86 16702 16473  0.9039
#>  converged boundary
#>       TRUE    FALSE
#>       TRUE     TRUE
#>       TRUE    FALSE
#>       TRUE     TRUE
#>       TRUE     TRUE
#>       TRUE     TRUE
#> Pick one by its name: get_candidate(x, "<candidate>").
get_best(grid)
#>           candidate n_profiles n_group_classes model log_likelihood n_parameters   aic   bic
#> 3 profiles2_groups2          2               2  <NA>          -8188           47 16471 16596
#>   bic_individual entropy converged boundary n_best_replicated warnings error
#> 3          16718   0.943      TRUE    FALSE                 5           <NA>

The BIC (Schwarz, 1978) selects two profiles and two group classes. That candidate has no estimate on a boundary and reaches its best log likelihood from every start; all candidates with three profiles have boundary estimates and reach their best solutions from a single start. A multilevel latent profile analysis of the same data favours additional group classes, which absorb the serial dependence that it does not model; LTA models that dependence and selects the generating structure.

Fit

The lta() function requires indicators (vars), a group identifier (id), and occasion order (time). The arguments n_profiles and n_group_classes specify the latent structure; n_starts and seed control repeated estimation from reproducible starting values.

moves <- lta(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
             time = "sequence", covariance_model = "full",
             n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
moves
#> Latent transition model: 2 profiles, 2 group classes
#> 1422 observations in 106 groups, up to 15 occasions (unbalanced, observed grid)
#> Log likelihood: -8188.367007; 47 parameters; BIC (groups): 16595.9157
#> Converged: TRUE after 18 iterations; best of 10 starts
#> Smallest standardized Gaussian eigenvalue: 0.27 (profiles, profile_2); Gaussian mass: 585; weight effective n: 600.5.
#> 
#> Class sizes   profile_1 58.9% (837)   profile_2 41.1% (585)
#> Group classes group_class_1 37.0% (39)   group_class_2 63.0% (67)
#> 
#> Means
#>   indicator profile_1 profile_2
#>      browse     0.538    -0.770
#>    lectures     0.423    -0.605
#>  forum_read     0.615    -0.879
#>  forum_post     0.528    -0.755
#>  attendance     0.635    -0.908
#> 
#> Variances and standard errors: get_results(x, "profiles").
#> Every other table: get_results(x, what = ), or get_results(x, "all").

Profile 1 (58.9% of the enrolments) lies 0.42 to 0.64 standard deviations above the course mean on all indicators and profile 2 (41.1%) 0.61 to 0.91 below it: engaged and disengaged enrolments.

The "starts" table reports the log likelihood reached by each start. Replication of the selected likelihood supports numerical stability but does not establish that the global maximum has been found.

get_results(moves, "starts")
#>    start log_likelihood converged iterations error
#> 1      1          -8188      TRUE         18  <NA>
#> 2      2          -8188      TRUE         21  <NA>
#> 3      3          -8188      TRUE         21  <NA>
#> 4      4          -8188      TRUE         24  <NA>
#> 5      5          -8188      TRUE         21  <NA>
#> 6      6          -8188      TRUE         24  <NA>
#> 7      7          -8188      TRUE         24  <NA>
#> 8      8          -8188      TRUE         21  <NA>
#> 9      9          -8188      TRUE         18  <NA>
#> 10    10          -8188      TRUE         21  <NA>

All ten starts reach the log likelihood of -8188.

Profiles

The profile plot displays estimated indicator means and the estimated share of occasions in each profile. For a transition model, plot() without an explicit view instead displays transition matrices.

plot_profiles(moves)

The profile heatmap expresses each mean in standard deviations from the indicator’s overall mean, facilitating comparison across indicators.

plot_profiles(moves, what = "heatmap")

Starting probabilities

The "initial" table reports initial profile probabilities (probability), profile prevalence across occasions (prevalence), and estimated group-class proportions (group_class_probability).

get_results(moves, "initial")
#>   group_class profile probability prevalence group_class_probability
#> 1           1       1       0.271      0.246                    0.37
#> 2           1       2       0.729      0.754                    0.37
#> 3           2       1       0.833      0.789                    0.63
#> 4           2       2       0.167      0.211                    0.63

Group class 2 (63% of the students) starts engaged with probability 0.833 and is engaged at 78.9% of its occasions; group class 1 (37%) starts engaged with probability 0.271 and is engaged at 24.6% of its occasions. These prevalences match the stationary probabilities of the committed and wavering students in the simulation, about 0.8 and 0.25.

Transitions

The "transitions" table reports the probability of moving from state from to state to at the next occasion. Probabilities sum to one within each origin state and group class. The column stable identifies transitions that retain the same state; expected_count reports the posterior expected transition count. A row with estimated = FALSE lacks information for estimating that transition distribution.

get_results(moves, "transitions")
#>   group_class from to probability expected_count origin_expected_count supported stable estimated
#> 1           1    1  1      0.7742           93.6                   121      TRUE   TRUE      TRUE
#> 2           1    1  2      0.2258           27.3                   121      TRUE  FALSE      TRUE
#> 3           1    2  1      0.0679           24.7                   364      TRUE  FALSE      TRUE
#> 4           1    2  2      0.9321          339.6                   364      TRUE   TRUE      TRUE
#> 5           2    1  1      0.8842          582.0                   658      TRUE   TRUE      TRUE
#> 6           2    1  2      0.1158           76.2                   658      TRUE  FALSE      TRUE
#> 7           2    2  1      0.4076           70.3                   173      TRUE  FALSE      TRUE
#> 8           2    2  2      0.5924          102.2                   173      TRUE   TRUE      TRUE
#>   group_class_probability
#> 1                    0.37
#> 2                    0.37
#> 3                    0.37
#> 4                    0.37
#> 5                    0.63
#> 6                    0.63
#> 7                    0.63
#> 8                    0.63

The group classes differ mainly in recovery from disengagement. A committed student (group class 2) who is disengaged in one course is engaged in the next with probability 0.408; a wavering student (group class 1) with probability 0.068, remaining disengaged with probability 0.932. Engagement is stable in both classes (0.884 and 0.774). Every transition rests on enough expected moves to be estimated (supported and estimated are TRUE).

The transition plot displays one matrix per group class, with current profiles in rows and next-occasion profiles in columns.

plot_transitions(moves)

Sequences

The sequence plot displays one row per group, coloured by the most probable profile at each occasion, as the sequence index plots of sequence analysis do (Saqr et al., 2024). These modal assignments summarize the fitted sequences but omit classification uncertainty.

plot_sequences(moves)

Classification

The "entropy" table reports relative entropy for occasions and groups (Ramaswamy et al., 1993). With more than one class, a value of 1 indicates certain posterior membership; 0 indicates equal posterior probabilities across classes for every case. Entropy summarizes classification separation under the fitted model.

get_results(moves, "entropy")
#>         level n_classes n_units entropy_sum relative_entropy
#> 1 individuals         2    1422        56.5            0.943
#> 2      groups         2     106        25.4            0.654

Occasions are classified clearly (0.943), students much less so (0.654). Under the transition model a student’s class rests on the dynamics of a sequence of 10 to 15 states, and a wavering student who happens to stay engaged for several courses resembles a committed one. The cross-tabulation with the generating labels shows the consequence.

get_results(moves, "assignments", data = course_engagement,
            truth = c("engagement", "student_type"))
#>    assignment class        truth      value   n proportion
#> 1     profile     1   engagement disengaged  10     0.0171
#> 2     profile     2   engagement disengaged 575     0.9829
#> 3     profile     1   engagement    engaged 825     0.9857
#> 4     profile     2   engagement    engaged  12     0.0143
#> 5 group_class     1 student_type  committed   1     0.0161
#> 6 group_class     2 student_type  committed  61     0.9839
#> 7 group_class     1 student_type   wavering  35     0.7955
#> 8 group_class     2 student_type   wavering   9     0.2045

The profiles recover 825 of the 837 engaged and 575 of the 585 disengaged enrolments (98.6% and 98.3%). Group class 2 contains 61 of the 62 committed students and 9 of the 44 wavering ones. Diagnostic plots display per-case uncertainty within each profile (what = "entropy") and posterior probabilities of assigned profiles (what = "posteriors").

plot_diagnostics(moves, what = "entropy")

plot_diagnostics(moves, what = "posteriors")

Transition networks

The estimated transitions can be represented as networks. get_tna() returns a network pooled across group classes; get_group_tna() returns one network per class. Both functions produce tna objects (Tikka et al., 2025) that can be displayed with plot() and analysed further with tna or with Nestimate (Saqr et al., 2026), which accepts tna and group_tna objects.

plot(get_tna(moves))

plot(get_group_tna(moves))

Beyond homogeneous transitions

Several extensions permit alternative specifications of temporal dependence and measurement:

  • transition_covariates lets covariates shift the transition probabilities: the log odds of moving to each other profile rather than staying. A covariate may change over occasions.
  • initial_covariates lets covariates shift the starting profile.
  • transitions = "occasion" estimates a separate transition matrix for each move.
  • measurement = "occasion" lets the profiles’ means and variances differ by occasion.
  • order = 2 makes the next profile depend on the two previous ones.
  • mover_stayer = TRUE adds a class of groups that never change profile (Goodman, 1961).

enumerate_classes(..., time = "sequence") compares numbers of profiles and group classes, and bootstrap_lrt() tests a model against a nested one.

The following example examines whether previous_grade, which varies across courses, is associated with transition probabilities:

grade <- lta(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
             time = "sequence", covariance_model = "full", n_profiles = 2,
             n_group_classes = 2, transition_covariates = "previous_grade",
             n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
get_results(grade, "transition_coefficients")
#>     group_class      from        to           term estimate standard_error statistic  p_value
#> 1 group_class_1 profile_1 profile_2    (Intercept)   -1.050          0.425    -2.471 1.35e-02
#> 2 group_class_1 profile_1 profile_2 previous_grade   -0.348          0.398    -0.876 3.81e-01
#> 3 group_class_1 profile_2 profile_1    (Intercept)   -2.756          0.453    -6.085 1.17e-09
#> 4 group_class_1 profile_2 profile_1 previous_grade   -0.211          0.340    -0.619 5.36e-01
#> 5 group_class_2 profile_1 profile_2    (Intercept)   -2.119          0.162   -13.047 6.64e-39
#> 6 group_class_2 profile_1 profile_2 previous_grade    0.206          0.162     1.276 2.02e-01
#> 7 group_class_2 profile_2 profile_1    (Intercept)   -0.297          0.282    -1.051 2.93e-01
#> 8 group_class_2 profile_2 profile_1 previous_grade    0.266          0.211     1.262 2.07e-01
#>   conf_low conf_high odds_ratio estimated
#> 1   -1.883    -0.217     0.3499      TRUE
#> 2   -1.128     0.432     0.7058      TRUE
#> 3   -3.643    -1.868     0.0636      TRUE
#> 4   -0.878     0.457     0.8100      TRUE
#> 5   -2.437    -1.801     0.1202      TRUE
#> 6   -0.111     0.523     1.2292      TRUE
#> 7   -0.849     0.256     0.7434      TRUE
#> 8   -0.147     0.680     1.3049      TRUE

The odds ratios of previous_grade are between 0.71 and 1.30, and every 95% interval of its log-odds coefficients includes zero. These results provide limited evidence of an association between previous grade and transitions in this example; they do not establish the absence of an association. A second-order model, in which the next profile depends on the two previous states, and a mover-stayer model can also be compared with the first-order specification using BIC:

second <- lta(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
              time = "sequence", covariance_model = "full", n_profiles = 2,
              n_group_classes = 2, order = 2, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
stayer <- lta(course_engagement, vars = vars, id = "student",
              time = "sequence", covariance_model = "full", n_profiles = 2,
              mover_stayer = TRUE, n_starts = 10, seed = 1)
BIC(moves, grade, second, stayer)
#>        df   BIC
#> moves  47 16596
#> grade  51 16611
#> second 55 16628
#> stayer 45 16606

For these data, BIC is lower for the first-order model with two group classes than for any extension: the grade covariate (BIC higher by 15), the second-order dependence (by 32) and the mover-stayer model with one class of movers (by 10). Extended models provide transition and initial-state logit coefficients, with Wald standard errors when supported by the fitted model, and occasion-specific probability summaries.

Assumptions

  • By default the next profile depends only on the current profile and the group class, and transition probabilities are the same at every occasion; the arguments above relax each of these.
  • Profiles have the same definition at every occasion unless measurement = "occasion".
  • Indicators are independent within a profile under the default diagonal covariance; covariance_model = "full" or a non-diagonal model relaxes it, as here.
